findings.text: The opening tells a newcomer what Athena is in two sentences. This is the only description of Athena on the page: no example request, no output, and no word on how to run it.
findings.source: Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost.

findings.text: This page is Athena's homepage URL, but almost all of it is about another project, firstmate. The lede does explain the switch. Still, someone who came to learn about Athena gets a long technical study of a tool they may not care about, and has to infer that the study is Athena's showcase.
findings.source: <title>Athena explains how firstmate handles work</title>; "This page is that study of firstmate."

findings.text: The page clearly says why the study exists, and it backs that up: 44 claims, each linked to file and line ranges at a fixed commit. A newcomer can check that the tracing is real.
findings.source: Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files.

findings.text: The next step is easy to find: it is linked from the header and has its own section. But it only points to the GitHub repo, so all install and usage details live off the page.
findings.source: Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself (header link to #next-steps); Next steps: "Learn about Athena, and how to install and try it: https://github.com/doodla/athena"

findings.text: The 'Start here' section is well built. It defines a few words first, then gives a plain account of firstmate, then numbers the steps one task goes through. A newcomer can follow that much.
findings.source: Start here: "The three parts below say what firstmate is, follow one piece of work, and say what happens when something fails or has no limit."

findings.text: Several terms are used without ever being defined: 'captain call', 'wake', 'endpoint' and 'durable record' have no Glossary entry. The Transitions cards get dense with them, so a stranger loses the thread there.
findings.source: t9: "Teardown finds the backlog item is still an open captain call"; t8: "A stale wake shows the worker is stuck ... a secondmate re-reads its pin ... a secondmate with no endpoint"

findings.text: Some Glossary definitions don't explain the word. 'Ship' is one of the main task kinds, yet its entry only says where the word appears, not what a ship is.
findings.source: Glossary, ship: "A kind of task, named next to scouts."

findings.text: The yolo, green and red rules are restated in nearly every section. This makes the page long and repetitive for a first-time reader without adding anything new.
findings.source: yolo is defined under "Words used first", again in "What firstmate is", in step 5, in t4, in t10 and in the Glossary

findings.text: The finding ids jump from f1 to f3, with no f2 and no explanation. A stranger can't tell whether something was left out.
findings.source: Limits of this study: items f1, f3, f4

findings.text: This sentence is awkward and points the reader around the page instead of simply giving the definitions, which appear right after it anyway.
findings.source: The two deciders are explained below the cards' heading.
